newsitem.title: zaire: U.S. says Zaire peace talks Friday, rebels advance.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Zaire peace talks Friday, rebels advance.

text.p: U.S. envoy Bill Richardson said Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila would hold their first face-to-face meeting on Friday on a South African navy ship in the Atlantic.
The rebels, who have seized over half of Zaire since October, advanced steadily towards the capital Kinshasa.

"The meeting will take place on Friday on a South African ship. The ship will be sailing from Libreville into international waters," Richardson said on Wednesday after one hour and 40 minutes of talks with Mobutu.

"This is an historic occasion that hopefully will lead to a peaceful transition in Zaire," the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations told reporters in Kinshasa after shuttling between Mobutu and Kabila since Tuesday.
It would be the first direct meeting between the ailing Zairean president and Kabila.
Asked if there were any preconditions for the talks, Richardson replied: "There are no preconditions for the talks."

Richardson stood beside Zairean Foreign Minister Kamanda wa Kamanda. Mobutu, looking gaunt and thin, stood behind him briefly in the doorway of the presidential villa in the heavily guarded Tshatshi military camp on the banks of the Zaire river.
Richardson said that several African leaders and joint U.N. and Organisation of African Unity envoy Mohamed Sahnoun would be present on the South African ship for the talks on Friday.

"I want to commend the statesmanlike action of President Mobutu and Mr Kabila in accepting these talks," said Richardson, adding Mobutu gave him a letter to U.S. President Bill Clinton in response to one he had delivered on Tuesday.
"It is our hope there will be a ceasefire while these talks take place," Richardson said. But he added this was a step-by -step process. Kabila has ruled out a ceasefire before talks.
Asked what caused Mobutu's change of heart on the venue from Gabon, which Kabila rejected on security grounds, Kamanda said: "It was a perception of the higher interest of the nation."
The meeting is expected to take place on the supply ship SAS Outeniqua, which is waiting off the coast of Zaire, and was to be chaired by South African President Nelson Mandela.
Richardson said part of the agreement was that he should attend the beginning of the talks and added in the next two days he might go on to South Africa, Gabon and possibly Angola.
Asked what the agenda for the talks was, Richardson said that would be discussed at the meeting. Kabila has said he wanted only a brief meeting to discuss Mobutu's stepping down.
Richardson said the talks would be under U.N. auspices but the United States "was proud to have played this catalyst role".
Earlier on Wednesday, Kabila appealed to the international community to force Mobutu to attend talks at sea to avoid a battle for Kinshasa, the teeming capital of five million people.
His rebels are massing at Kikwit, a major town they entered on Tuesday and which is 400 km (250 miles) east of Kinshasa.
Residents of Bumba, more than 1,000 km (625 miles) northeast of the capital, said in radio contacts with Kinshasa on Wednesday rebels had taken control without a fight.
Mobutu's home town of Lisala, west of Bumba, was also in imminent danger of capture, residents there said by radio.
Mobutu, who had prostate cancer surgery in Europe in August and met Richardson on Tuesday, had earlier baulked at the idea of talks at sea, a diplomat with the U.S. envoy said.
South African Deputy Foreign Minister Pahad said the naval vessel was a compromise venue close to Zaire where Mobutu and Kabila, suspicious of each other, could be assured of safety.
Before the meeting was announced, an airlift home of Rwandan refugees from rebel-held Zaire began on Wednesday but hit problems when a fuel shortage grounded more than two flights.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said 186 unaccompanied refugee children left Kisangani's international airport for Rwanda's capital on one plane and 50 more refugees on another aircraft.
Richardson has questioned the rebels' human rights record and said the world wants an investigation of allegations of a massacre of refugees by Zairean villagers and rebels last week.
On a brief visit to Kisangani before flying to Kinshasa on Wednesday, he waded into a crowd of Rwandan Hutu refugees in Zaire all smiles and handshakes.
He stopped in front of a young Hutu woman and gently stroked the brow of the child she was carrying.
"She's cold," he said. "She's dead," the mother replied.
